::: proof

Expanding entry-wise, $\tp{\vcoef} \matr{S} \vcoef = \sumjp \sumto{k}{p} s_{jk} \coef{j} \coef{k}$.
Differentiating component-wise with respect to $\coef{i}$ for $i = 1, \ldots, p$:

$$
\ba
\left[\deriv{\vcoef}(\tp{\vcoef}\matr{S}\vcoef)\right]_i
&= \deriv{\coef{i}} \sumjp \sumto{k}{p} s_{jk} \coef{j} \coef{k}
&& \text{(expand quadratic form)} \\
&= \sumto{k}{p} s_{ik} \coef{k} + \sumjp s_{ji} \coef{j}
&& \text{(product rule for } \coef{i} \coef{k} \text{)} \\
&= [\matr{S}\vcoef]_i + [\tp{\matr{S}}\vcoef]_i
&& \text{(matrix-vector multiplication definition)} \\
&= [(\matr{S} + \tp{\matr{S}})\vcoef]_i
&& \text{(linearity of matrix multiplication)}
\ea
$$

When $\matr{S}$ is symmetric ($\matr{S} = \tp{\matr{S}}$), $\matr{S} + \tp{\matr{S}} = 2\matr{S}$, so $\deriv{\vcoef}(\tp{\vcoef}\matr{S}\vcoef) = 2\matr{S}\vcoef$.

:::
